synopsis: The corpus frames collision-mitigation tuning as constrained multi-objective optimization: missed or late interventions are hard constraints, while nuisance warnings, unnecessary braking and productivity loss remain visible on a Pareto front for accountable safety-policy selection [f136, f6672, f14442]. Excessive conservatism can create alarm fatigue, productivity loss and intervention-created hazards, and operators switching off nuisance-heavy systems gives unnecessary braking a safety significance rather than merely an economic cost [f6569, f14416, f14441]. Evolutionary methods including NSGA-II, attributed to Deb and colleagues in 2002, expose the frontier and support parallel simulation, while multi-objective Bayesian variants cited in 2024 seek the frontier with sample-efficient selection; the identified evidence is generic engineering rather than specific off-road braking evidence [f6970, f14420, f6975, f7324, f7322]. Evolutionary tuning requires many evaluations and carries over-fitting risk, so the booklet recommends nested validation, pre-declared safety constraints for final-point selection and independent confirmation; operational evidence establishing optimum braking conservatism remains thin [f7319, f7320, f7321, f6570]. In the illustrative zero-miss example, A has 2 unnecessary brakes per 100 hours and a generous stopping margin, whereas B has 0.5 per 100 hours and a thinner margin; selecting between them is a safety-policy decision [f14406, f14407, f14408, f14411]. The example also declares C dominated, but its stated comparisons—less margin than A and more nuisance braking than B—do not alone establish that one alternative is at least as good on every objective, leaving the dominance explanation incomplete [f14404, f14409, f14410].

relations.note: Both require visible Pareto trade-offs for engineers and safety authorities.
Both make Pareto-point selection an explicit safety-policy decision rather than a hidden weight.
Both recommend preserving and displaying the Pareto frontier.
Both identify parallel simulation evaluation as an advantage of evolutionary Pareto methods.
Many evaluations are an additional burden beyond the unresolved Pareto-point policy choice.
Producing the whole frontier in one run still leaves acceptable-point selection to policy.
Both match evolutionary tuning to misses, nuisance braking and stopping-margin trade-offs.
Safe Bayesian variants additionally restrict exploration to settings believed safe.
Both recommend constrained optimization with visible safety trade-offs.
Subjective desirability weights support avoiding hidden safety valuations in a single cost.
Explicit trade-offs explain why the frontier should remain visible rather than collapsed.
Conservative-trigger harms justify joint safety and productivity acceptance criteria.
Operator shutdown evidence supports including human-factors rates in multi-objective tuning.
Margin-versus-nuisance tension motivates balancing stopping margin and unnecessary braking.
Single-objective failures are explained through shutdown risk and missed hazards.
Trying many configurations motivates nested validation and independent confirmation.
Choosing between illustrative frontier settings demonstrates the remaining safety-policy decision.
Generic methodological strengths do not establish specific off-road evidence.
